hints: Focus on what makes a carbon chiral, four different single-bonded groups with no double bond and no two identical substituents.
Look first at carbon 2 and carbon 3, carbon 2 is part of a C=C double bond and carbon 3 is joined to two identical methyl groups.
Check carbon 1 carefully, it has OH, an isopropyl group, and two ring paths that are different because the double bond is off-centre, giving four different groups.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for a chiral centre**

A chiral carbon must be sp3, with four single bonds to four different atoms or groups.

Any $C=C$ carbon cannot be chiral, and any carbon with two identical groups cannot be chiral.

**Test carbon 2**

Carbon 2 is one end of the double bond in the ring and is also bonded to a methyl group.

It has only three bonded groups and is planar sp2, so $$\text{carbon 2 is not chiral}$$

**Test carbon 3**

Carbon 3 is the $CH$ of the isopropyl group, bonded to carbon 1, to H, and to two $CH_3$ groups.

Because the two methyl groups are identical, $$\text{carbon 3 is not chiral}$$

**Test carbon 1**

Carbon 1 is sp3 and bonded to $OH$, to carbon 3 of the isopropyl group, to the left $CH_2$ of the ring and to the right $CH_2$ of the ring.

The left and right ring routes back to carbon 2 are different, one meets the double bond after one $CH_2$ and the other after two $CH_2$ groups, so all four groups are different. Therefore only carbon 1 is chiral.

options.A: Incorrect. This suggests all three labelled carbons are chiral. Carbon 2 fails because it is sp2 in C=C, and carbon 3 fails because it carries two identical methyl groups.
options.B: Incorrect. Carbon 2 is an alkene carbon bonded to a methyl group and two ring carbons. With a double bond and only three groups it cannot have four different single bonds.
options.C: Incorrect. This includes carbon 3. Carbon 3 is $CH(CH_3)_2$, the two $CH_3$ groups are identical, so it does not have four different groups even though carbon 1 in this option is chiral.
options.D: Correct. Only carbon 1 has four different single-bonded groups: OH, $CH(CH_3)_2$, and two non-equivalent $CH_2$ ring segments made different by the unsymmetrical position of the double bond.
